en: Mahāniddesa,
Aṭṭhakavagga 12.
Cūḷabyūhasuttaniddesa (The Exposition of the Shorter Discourse on the Great Battle)
Now he will explain the exposition of the Cūḷabyūhasutta:
"Each adhering to their own respective views,
they dispute, each claiming to be skillful."
He who knows thus understands the Dhamma;
he who rejects this is incomplete.
They remain clinging to their own respective views.
There are some recluses and brahmins who are followers of speculative views;
having adopted, mastered, grasped, clung to, and adhered to one or another of the sixty-two types of speculative views, they dwell, live together, abide, and persist in their respective views.
Just as householders dwell in houses, or those with offenses dwell amidst offenses, or those with defilements dwell amidst defilements; so do they dwell in their respective views.
This being so, some ascetics and brahmins who follow various speculative views,
having taken up, mastered, grasped, clung to, and adhered to one or another of the sixty-two types of speculative views,
dwell, live together, reside, and abide according to their respective views.
"Each adhering to their own respective views.
"Having quarreled, those skilled in various ways speak":

"having quarreled" means having grasped, taken up, seized, clung to, and become dogmatically attached; they speak in various ways, they speak diversely, they speak against one another, they speak separately; they do not speak as one, but rather they discourse, utter, illuminate, and express themselves [thus].

"Those who speak of the wholesome (kusala) are speakers of the wholesome, speakers of wisdom, speakers of stability, speakers of the method, speakers of cause, speakers of characteristics, speakers of reason, speakers of the ground;
according to their own tenets, they dispute and speak variously of what is wholesome.
He who knows thus, he understands the Dhamma."
"He who knows this Dhamma, this view, this way, this path— he has known, understood, seen, and penetrated the Dhamma"—
he who knows thus has known the Dhamma.
"He is one who rejects this" means he is incomplete.

"He who rejects this Dhamma, this view, this practice, this path—he is incomplete, he is unperfected, he is unfulfilled; he is inferior, base, lowly, contemptible, wretched, fourfold, and limited"—this is what is meant by "he who rejects is incomplete.
Therefore, he was called "the created one" (so nimmito).
“Each clinging to their own respective views,
they dispute, each claiming to be skilled.
He who knows thus— he understands the Dhamma.”
"He who opposes this is not a whole person.
Thus they dispute, quarreling with one another,
saying, "The other is a fool, he is unskilled."
"Which of these claims is true?
For all of them proclaim themselves to be skilled.
Thus they quarrel and dispute."
Having thus grasped, mastered, seized, clung to, and adhered to it, they dispute, engage in quarreling, engage in brawling, engage in contention, engage in strife, and engage in conflict, saying:
"You do not understand this Dhamma and Vinaya... [etc.
...either explain it yourself if you can!"
Thus they quarrel and dispute.
They say, "The other is foolish and unskilled.

They say, "The other is foolish, inferior, base, lowly, contemptible, wretched, limited, unskilled, ignorant, enveloped in ignorance, lacking knowledge, without discernment, and of poor wisdom. Thus they have said, thus they speak, thus they declare, thus they illuminate, and thus they express themselves.
"The other is a fool and unskilled"—
which of these claims is true?
Among these recluses and brahmins, which claim is true, real, factual, actual, as it is, and not otherwise?
"Which among these is the true doctrine?
For all of them indeed proclaim what is wholesome.

All these recluses and brahmins proclaim what is wholesome; they are speakers of wisdom, speakers of stability, speakers of the method, speakers of cause, speakers of characteristics, speakers of reason, speakers of grounds, according to their own respective tenets."
"All these indeed are speakers of what is wholesome.
Therefore that created being said:
"Even thus they quarrel and dispute."
"The other is a fool and unskilled," they say.
Which of these statements is true?
For all of them claim to be skilled.
If a fool does not approve of the Dhamma of another,
he is base and of inferior wisdom;
indeed, all fools are of very inferior wisdom.
All these are obsessed by views.
If they do not approve of another’s Dhamma— by not approving,
not observing, not consenting, not acquiescing, and not rejoicing in another’s Dhamma, view, practice, and path— [they are thus obsessed].
"If one does not approve of another's Dhamma, that fool is base, inferior in wisdom.

Herein, "the other is a fool" means he is base, inferior, low, contemptible, fourfold, and limited; he is inferior in wisdom, inferior in wisdom, base in wisdom, contemptible in wisdom, fourfold in wisdom, and limited in wisdom.
He is dull-witted and of inferior wisdom.
All these fools are indeed of very inferior wisdom.

All these recluses and brahmins are fools, inferior, lowly, base, contemptible, mediocre, and limited; they are all of inferior wisdom, of very inferior wisdom, of low wisdom, of base wisdom, of contemptible wisdom, and of limited wisdom.
"All these fools are of utterly inferior wisdom.
All these are mired in views.
All these ascetics and brahmins are followers of speculative views.
Having taken up, grasped, seized, clung to, and adhered to one or another of these sixty-two views, they dwell, live together, abide, and persist in their respective views.

Just as householders dwell in houses, or those with offenses dwell in their offenses, or those with defilements dwell in their defilements—even so do all these recluses and brahmins who hold to views... [as above]... dwell, live together, abide, and persist in their respective views.
"They dwell around"—
all these indeed dwell around views.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“The fool who does not approve of the Dhamma of another is base and of inferior wisdom;
indeed, all fools are of very inferior wisdom.”
"All these are merely entangled in views.
Yet they are pure in their own view, cleansed,
possessing purified wisdom, skillful, and wise.
Not one among them has lost his wisdom,
for their views are likewise fully perfected;
they possess direct vision and are thoroughly purified.
“With their own views, with their own inclinations, with their own preferences, with their own convictions, they are not clear, not pure, not cleansed, defiled, and subject to defilement”— thus,
because of their own views, they are not clear.
They are those of purified wisdom, skilled, and wise.
Pure wisdom, purified wisdom, completely purified wisdom, cleansed wisdom, thoroughly cleansed wisdom; or alternatively,
pure vision, purified vision, completely purified vision, cleansed vision, thoroughly cleansed vision— this is "wisdom that is well-cleansed."
“Skilled” means skilled, wise, possessed of wisdom, possessed of psychic power, possessed of knowledge, discerning, and intelligent— thus the skilled ones possess purified wisdom.
“Possessed of intelligence” means possessed of intelligence, wise, possessed of wisdom, possessed of psychic power, possessed of knowledge, discerning, and intelligent.
"Purified in wisdom, skillful, and possessed of mindfulness.

Among those ascetics and brahmins, there is no one whose wisdom has declined, no one of inferior wisdom, no one of debased wisdom, no one of low wisdom, no one of base wisdom, no one of mediocre wisdom, and no one of limited wisdom.
All of them possess the best wisdom, distinguished wisdom, preeminent wisdom, supreme wisdom,
and excellent wisdom; among them, there is none whose wisdom has declined,
for their views are likewise fully perfected.
The view of those recluses and brahmins is thus fully undertaken, adopted, grasped, adhered to, clung to, and intent upon;
for their view is indeed thus fully undertaken.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Those who are directly visible, stainless,
with purified wisdom, skillful, and mindful—
among them, no one has lost their wisdom.”
"For their views are likewise held with such conviction.
Nor do I say that what fools call "this is the truth" to one another is actually so.
Each made their own view the truth;
therefore they regard the other as a fool,
saying, "I do not say this is the reality."
This is not a rejection.

As for this: "The sixty-two views, I say of them: 'This is not true, this is not such, this is not real, this is not as it is, this is not unperverted'—I declare, I explain, I teach, I prescribe, I establish, I reveal, I analyze, I make plain, I manifest, I proclaim"—it is not that I say, "This is not such."
"Those whom fools call 'mutually'":
"Mutually" means two persons, two who cause strife, two who cause quarrels, two who cause disputes, two who cause litigation, two disputants, two who engage in debate;

they say of one another, "He is a fool, inferior, base, lowly, wretched, deficient, and limited," thus they speak, thus they converse, thus they declare, thus they explain, thus they express themselves.
Fools call one another mutually "this is true," each making their own respective view the truth:
"The world is eternal; this alone is the truth, all else is false."
Each made their own respective view the truth:
“The world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false”… [and so on] … “A Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is true, all else is false.”
Each made their own view the truth.
Therefore, they regard another as a fool. "Therefore" means:

for that reason, on that account, by that cause, by that condition, and with that as the source, they regard, see, perceive, look upon, contemplate, and examine another as a fool—one who is inferior, base, lowly, wretched, deficient, and limited.
Therefore, they burn others, saying, "He is a fool.
For this reason the Blessed One said:
"I do not say that this is the truth."
"Those whom the foolish call 'each other,' each making their own view the truth—
therefore they are called 'fools' because they disparage others."
What some call truth and reality,
others call empty and false;
thus they quarrel and dispute.
"Why do the recluses not say one and the same thing?
Why is it that some say, 'This is the truth, this is so'?
Regarding whatever doctrine, view, practice, or path some recluses and brahmins declare: "This is the truth, this is real, this is so..."
"Real, as it is, and not otherwise"—thus some say, thus they speak, thus they declare, thus they illuminate, thus they express:
"That which they call truth and reality.
But others say that this is empty and false.
Regarding that very same Dhamma, view, practice, and path, some recluses and brahmins say:

"This is empty, this is false, this is unreal, this is deceptive, this is not as it truly is"; thus they speak, thus they discourse, thus they declare, thus they illuminate, thus they express themselves.
They say of that as well: "It is empty; it is false.
Thus they quarrel and dispute.
Having thus grasped, taken up, seized, clung to, and adhered to [their views], they dispute, engage in strife, engage in brawling, engage in quarreling, and engage in contention.
“You do not understand this Dhamma and Vinaya...
[as before] ...or unravel it if you are able”—
in this way they quarrel and dispute.
"Why do the recluses not speak of one [thing]?"—here "why" (*kasmā*) means for what reason, for what cause, for what condition, for what source, for what origin, for what birth, for what arising;
why do they not speak of one, but speak of many, speak diversely, speak variously, speak separately, and speak at length? They explain it thus.
"They speak, they illuminate, they express"—why do the recluses not say this of one [person]?
Therefore he said: "He is the created one."
“Some say that what is true is suchness,
while others say it is empty and false;
thus they quarrel and dispute.”
"Why do the recluses not speak of one [truth]?
For there is but one truth, and no second exists,
concerning which those who understand do not dispute.
"Various truths you yourself proclaim;
therefore, recluses do not speak of one [truth].
For there is but one truth, and no second."
One truth is said to be the cessation of suffering, Nibbāna.
That which is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.
Or alternatively, one truth is said to be:
The truth of the path, the truth of the outlet, the practice leading to the cessation of suffering, the noble eightfold path, namely: right view, right intention,
right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—
for there is indeed one truth, and no second exists.
"In that which people do not dispute, they understand.
"In that" means in that truth.
"People" is a designation for sentient beings.
Those who understand that truth— understanding it, knowing it, fully comprehending it, and penetrating it—
would not engage in quarreling, would not engage in brawling, would not engage in contention, would not engage in dispute,
and would not engage in strife; they would abandon, dispel, and eliminate quarreling, brawling, contention, dispute, and strife.
“They would bring about its disappearance, they would lead it to non-existence”—
this is that which people do not dispute among those who understand.
“They each proclaim their own various truths,” so it is said.
They themselves chant, speak, converse, declare, illuminate, and express various truths:
"The world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false"—thus they themselves chant, speak, converse, declare, illuminate, and express.
"The world is not eternal... [and so forth].

“The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is the truth, all else is vain”—thus they themselves praise, speak, discourse, declare, illuminate, and express these various truths.
Therefore, it is said that ascetics do not speak with one voice.

Therefore, for that reason, by that cause, by that condition, by that source, they do not speak as one; they speak diversely, they speak variously, they speak differently from one another, they speak separately; they declare, they utter, they illuminate, they express—thus, for that reason, the recluses do not speak as one.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“There is indeed one truth, there is no second;
regarding that which people who understand do not dispute,
they themselves proclaim various truths.”
"Therefore, the recluses do not say that there is one [truth].
Why indeed do they speak of truths as manifold?
They proclaim them, being skilled in speaking.
Many truths have been heard in various ways;
do they perhaps rely on reasoning?
Why, then, do they speak of truths as being diverse?

"Kasmā" means for what reason, for what cause, for what condition, for what source? Why do they speak of the truths diversely, speak of them variously, speak of them differently from one another, speak of them as manifold, declare, utter, illuminate, and express them?
"Why indeed do they speak of the truths diversely? [The answer is:
"Because they proclaim themselves to be skilled in speaking."
They dispute, they argue; thus they are called "disputants" (*pavādiyāse*).
Alternatively, they proclaim, speak, say, illuminate, and express their respective positions (*diṭṭhigata*):
they proclaim, speak, say, illuminate, and express [the view], "The world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false."
“The world is eternal” … [and so on] … “the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is true, all else is false”—thus they proclaim, speak, utter, illuminate, and express.

They are speakers of what is wholesome, speakers of wisdom, speakers of the learned, speakers of the firm, speakers of the methodical, speakers of causes, speakers of characteristics, speakers of reasons, speakers of grounds, and speakers according to their own tenets.
They proclaimed themselves as speakers of what is skillful.
"Many truths heard, various" means many truths have been heard that are diverse, manifold, mutually distinct,
and extensive— thus, "many truths heard, various."
"Or do they recollect reasoning? means: "Or do they proceed, lead, drift, and are carried away by reasoning and intention?
In this way, too, they recollect reasoning.
Or else, they speak, say, utter, illuminate, and express what is struck by reasoning, followed by investigation, and arisen from their own intuition.
"Or do they perhaps rely on their own reasoning?
Thus that created being said:
"Why indeed do they speak of truths diversely?"
"You who speak skillfully,
you have heard many various truths.
Or do you merely rely on reasoning?"
There are not indeed many various truths in the world,
apart from perception; for having fashioned out reasoning within one's own views, [one clings to them].
"Truth and falsehood"—thus they speak of two things.
"Not indeed many truths, nor various," means: not indeed many truths, nor various, nor diverse, nor mutually distinct, nor manifold—thus, "not indeed many truths, nor various."

Apart from perception, one regards nothing in the world as permanent; apart from perception, one does not grasp at anything in the world as permanent. Only one thing is spoken of, declared, illustrated, and designated in the world as true:
the cessation of suffering, Nibbāna.
That which is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.
Or else, one truth is called the truth of the path, the truth of deliverance, the practice leading to the cessation of suffering, the noble eightfold path; that is to say:
right view ... [and so on] ... right concentration—apart from perception, there are no eternal things in the world.
"Having fashioned their own reasoning among views, they proclaim the two-fold doctrine of 'truth' and 'falsehood.
Having reasoned, reflected, and intended; having reasoned upon, reflected upon, and intended upon, they give rise to, produce, generate, and bring forth into being various speculative views.

Having given rise to, produced, generated, and brought forth these speculative views, they say, "My [view] is the truth, yours is false. Thus they speak, thus they discourse, thus they utter, thus they illuminate, and thus they communicate.
Having fashioned out their own reasoning within various views, they speak of two things: truth and falsehood.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"There are not indeed many and diverse truths..."
Apart from perception, there are no eternal things in the world;
having fashioned arguments regarding views, they speak of two things: truth and falsehood.
Whether regarding what is seen, heard, customary observances, or what is sensed,
one who looks down with pride relying on these—
standing upon such judgment and laughing—
And he says, "The other is a fool, unskilled.
Relying on what is seen, heard, on moral habits, vows, or what is sensed, he looks down with pride.
Whether it be what is seen or purification through what is seen, what is heard or purification through what is heard, moral habit or purification through moral habit, or a vow—

"Or by relying on, depending on, grasping, misapprehending, and adhering to purification of conduct, or purification of observances, or purification of what is seen, or purification of what is heard, or purification of what is sensed, or purification of what is cognized—thus:
'in what is seen, heard, [conducted,] sensed, or cognized.
And by relying on these, one is a 'viewer of celestial mansions.'"
"He does not honor," thus he is one who sees with contempt;
or else, "he generates mental distress," thus he is one who sees with contempt—
relying on these things seen, heard, on virtuous conduct, or on what is sensed, he is one who sees with contempt.
"Standing in judgment, laughing":
here "judgments" refers to the sixty-two types of speculative views (*diṭṭhigata*).

Standing in the judgment of views—that is, having established oneself, having grasped, having clung to, and having adhered to—the view of judgment—it means: having stood, having established oneself, having taken hold of, having misapprehended, and having become dogmatically attached.
"Standing in judgment.
"Laughing" means he is satisfied, joyful, exultant, glad at heart, and one whose intentions are fulfilled.
Alternatively, "laughing with bared teeth"—
Standing in judgment and laughing, he says, "The other is a fool, unskilled. He says this:

"The other is a fool, inferior, base, lowly, wretched, deficient, limited, unskilled, ignorant, possessed by ignorance, lacking knowledge, without discernment, lacking wisdom, and devoid of understanding"—thus he speaks, thus he declares, thus he proclaims, thus he illuminates, thus he expresses himself.
And he says, "The other is a fool, unskilled.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"In what is seen, heard, in moral conduct, vows, or what is sensed..."
Relying on these, he looks down upon others from his celestial mansion;
standing in judgment, he laughs and says,
"The other is a fool, unskilled."
By the very fact that he disparages another as a fool,
he declares himself to be skilled; thus, by his own doing,
he proclaims himself to be one who is virtuous.
"He despises another; that itself is his downfall.
By whatever cause, by whatever condition, by whatever reason, and by whatever source he regards another as a fool, as inferior, or as base—by that very means he brings about his own downfall.
"He judges, sees, perceives, looks at, contemplates, and examines [the other] as inferior, base, fourfold, and limited"—thus he judges the other as "a fool.
Therefore, he says of himself: "I am skilled."
"Ātumāna" is said to mean "self. For that very reason,
by that cause, by that condition, by that motive, and by that origin, one regards oneself as "I am skilled, wise, intelligent, discerning, knowledgeable, experienced, and sagacious"— thus,
by means of that self-conceit, one says, "I am skilled."
“He himself proclaims what is wholesome”:

he himself proclaims for himself that which is a wholesome teaching, a wise teaching, a firm teaching, a reasoned teaching, a causal teaching, a characteristic-based teaching, a rational teaching, a foundational teaching,
according to his own tenets— thus, “he himself proclaims what is wholesome.”
"He despises another; he praises that very same person.
"He does not honor him correctly" also means he despises another.
Or alternatively, "he generates mental distress" also means he despises another.

He proclaims that very same thing, he proclaims that very same speculative view, thinking: "Thus this person is one of wrong view, of perverted vision"—he despises another while proclaiming that very same thing.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“By the very same means by which he brands another as a fool,
he calls himself skilled; though he proclaims himself to be virtuous, he is himself unskilled.”
"He despises another, yet it is he himself who is impure.
Consumed by the view of extreme asceticism,
intoxicated by pride, he is full of arrogance.
He has himself been consecrated by his own mind;
for that view is fully adopted by him.
He is one who has fully adopted an excessive view.
The sixty-two types of views are called "excessive views.
For what reason are the sixty-two types of views called "excessive views"?
Because all those views transcend cause, transcend characteristic, and transcend the proper place; for that reason, the sixty-two types of views are called "excessive views."
All sectarians, too, hold views that exceed [the truth].
For what reason do all sectarians hold views that exceed [the truth]?

Because they produce, generate, bring forth, and manifest speculative views by transgressing, surpassing, and going beyond one another; for that reason, all sectarians hold views that exceed [the truth].
“He is complete through the view of transcendence”:
he is complete and fulfilled through the view of transcendence, thus “he is complete through the view of transcendence.
He is called “Anoma” because he is complete through the view of transcendence.
"Intoxicated by conceit, full of pride": intoxicated,
heedless, crazed, and excessively drunk by means of his own view through the conceit of views—
this is "intoxicated by conceit."
"Full of conceit" means one who is full of conceit, complete with conceit,
possessed of unsurpassed conceit— one intoxicated by conceit,
full of conceit. He has himself, by his own mind, consecrated himself.

One sprinkles oneself with one’s own mind, thinking: “I am skilled, wise, discerning, intelligent, knowledgeable, insightful, and sagacious”—thus one is personally and directly consecrated by the mind.
For that view has been fully adopted by him in such a manner.
That view of his is thus fulfilled, undertaken, grasped, adhered to, settled upon, clung to, and resolved upon;
for that view of his is thus fulfilled.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Complete with the view of extreme laxity,
intoxicated by conceit and full of pride,
he has himself personally anointed his own mind.”
"For that view has been fully adopted by him.
If one is inferior because of another's words,
he himself becomes inferior in wisdom.
But if one is oneself a wise man of realized knowledge,
there is no fool among the ascetics. For if, on account of another’s words—

that is, because of another’s speech, because of being censured, because of being reviled, because of being slandered— one thinks that another is a fool, inferior, base, lowly, wretched, contemptible, or insignificant— then [one is not truly wise].
If one is inferior to another because of their speech,
one is a companion who is inferior in wisdom.
That person too, for that very reason, is a companion who is inferior in wisdom— one of low wisdom, base wisdom, wretched wisdom, deficient wisdom, limited wisdom, and meager wisdom.
One who is dull-witted is of inferior wisdom.
But if one is oneself a master of knowledge and wise— if one is oneself a master of knowledge, wise, learned, possessed of wisdom, intelligent, knowledgeable, discerning, and sagacious—
then one is oneself a master of knowledge and wise.
"There is no fool among the recluses.

Among the recluses there is no one who is foolish, inferior, base, lowly, wretched, deficient, or limited; rather, all possess the highest wisdom, distinguished wisdom, preeminent wisdom, supreme wisdom, and excellent wisdom—thus, "there is no fool among the recluses."
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“If one is indeed inferior to another in speech,
And is likewise inferior in wisdom, he is truly lowly.”
But if there is one who is himself a wise master of knowledge,
then there is no fool among the recluses.
Those who profess a doctrine other than this—
They have failed and do not possess complete purity;
even so, the sectarians speak thus individually,
for they are stained by attachment to their own direct perception.
"Those who profess a doctrine other than this have missed the path to purity;

they are incomplete. Those who profess a doctrine, a view, a way, or a path other than this have missed, failed, stumbled, and fallen away from the path of purity, the path of cleansing, the path of complete purification, the bright path, and the perfectly radiant path.

"Having understood [this], they have failed; they are incomplete, they are unfinished, they are unperfected, inferior, base, low, wretched, contemptible, and limited—those who proclaim a doctrine other than this, they have failed and their purity is incomplete.
Thus do the various sectarian teachers speak individually.
"Standpoint" (tittha) refers to a speculative view (diṭṭhigata).
"Forders" (titthiyā) refers to those who hold speculative views (diṭṭhigatikā).
They speak, converse, declare, elucidate, and express various views and various speculative positions—thus they are called "forders."
In this way, too, the sectarian teachers speak individually.
For they are "colored" by the passion for their own views;
they are stained, deeply stained, by the passion for their own views.
For they are stained by the lust for what is visible.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Those who profess a doctrine other than this..."
“They have failed and do not possess complete purity;
thus do the various sectarians speak,
for they are stained by attachment to what is directly perceived.”
"Here alone is purity," they proclaim;
they do not say that purity lies in other teachings.
Thus are the various sectarians firmly attached [to their own views].
"Insisting firmly on their own doctrines there:
'Purity is found only here,' they say.
Here they speak of purity, purification, complete purification; they speak of liberation, deliverance, and total release; they declare, explain, recite, illuminate, and express [these things].

“‘The world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false’—here they speak of, tell, say, illuminate, and express purification, complete purification, utter purification, liberation, complete liberation, and total liberation.
‘The world is non-eternal...
[and so on] ...neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is true, all else is false’—here they speak of purification...”
They speak of, talk about, declare, illuminate, and express purification, complete purification, liberation, emancipation, and total emancipation;
thus they proclaim purity right here.
They do not claim purification in other doctrines.
Setting aside their own teacher, Dhamma, Saṅgha, view, practice, and path, they cast asunder, uproot, and surround all opposing doctrines, saying:
"That teacher is not omniscient; the Dhamma is not well-expounded; the Saṅgha is not well-practiced; the view is not auspicious;
the practice is not well-proclaimed; the path is not leading to liberation; herein there is no purity, no purification, nor complete purification."
"Whether it be purity, liberation, or complete liberation—herein there is no cleansing, no purifying, no thorough purification;
nor is there any being released, liberated, or completely released;
[these things] are inferior, base, low, wretched, fourfold, and limited"—thus they have said, thus they speak, thus they declare, thus they illuminate, thus they express themselves.
They do not say that purity lies in other things.
Thus, the sectarians are settled in various ways.
"Tīrtha" (ford) is said to mean a speculative view.
"Tīrthikas" refers to those who hold wrong views.
Because they have settled, established, adhered, approached, clung to, and become intent upon various views among those who have gone to various views,
for this reason also the tīrthikas are "settled separately."
“They speak firmly on their own tenets therein”:

the Dhamma is one’s own tenet, the view is one’s own tenet, the practice is one’s own tenet, the path is one’s own tenet. Being firm-speakers, steadfast-speakers, powerful-speakers, and settled-speakers regarding their own tenets—thus, “they speak firmly on their own tenets therein.”
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Right here they proclaim purity; they do not say that purification lies in other things.”
"Even so, the sectarian teachers are individually settled,
firmly proclaiming their own doctrines therein.
Even while firmly proclaiming their own doctrines,"
Why should a fool burn another?
He brings that very destruction upon himself by speaking of another as a fool whose nature is impure.
"One who speaks firmly even regarding one's own position" (*sakāyane vāpi daḷhaṃ vadāno*):

the Dhamma is one's own position, a view is one's own position, the practice is one's own position, and the path is one's own position. One who is firm in speaking, steadfast in speaking, powerful in speaking, and resolute in speaking regarding one's own position is "one who speaks firmly even regarding one's own position."
"What does 'the fool here would burn another' mean?
Herein, according to his own view, his own inclination, his own preference, and his own doctrine, what [person] would he burn,
what would he regard as inferior, base, lowly, contemptible, wretched, fourth-rate, or insignificant?"
"Whom should one look at? Whom should one gaze upon? Whom should one contemplate?
Whom should one examine?"—in this regard, whom would a fool burn by calling another a fool?
He brings destruction upon himself by saying of another, "This fool is of an impure nature."
"One who says: 'The other is a fool, inferior, base, lowly, wretched, contemptible, fourfold, limited, of an impure nature, of an unpurified nature, of an unclean nature,
of an unwholesome nature'— speaking thus, talking thus, saying thus, illuminating thus, and declaring thus,
he himself would bring about, fully bring about, produce, fully produce, and drag in quarrels, disputes, conflicts, contentions, and strife."
"He would draw near, seize, grasp, and adhere"—
thus he himself brings about his own destruction by speaking of another as a fool whose nature is impure.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Even if one speaks firmly in defense of one’s own doctrine,
why should a fool burn another?
He only brings destruction upon himself.”
Speaking ill of another who is impure by nature,
having himself fallen into error while standing in judgment,
he incites further dispute in the world above.
Having abandoned all disputes,
a person does not create strife in the world;
by standing in dispute, one brings about one's own ruin.
"Judgments" (vinicchaya) refers to the sixty-two types of speculative views.
"Having stood upon, established oneself in, grasped, clung to, and adhered to the view of judgment" means having stood upon judgment.
"Having measured for oneself" means having measured by oneself.
Having personally measured and evaluated it, [thinking]: "This Teacher is omniscient;
this Dhamma is well-expounded;
this Saṅgha is practicing rightly..."
"This view is auspicious...
this practice is well-proclaimed...
this path leads to liberation"—having thus measured by measuring oneself.
"Standing in legal judgment, having himself erred,
he enters into dispute in the world beyond. Here,
"one who rises up" (uddhaṁsa) refers to the future.
Having set aside his own position, he himself engages in, approaches, draws near to, takes up, clings to, and adheres to quarreling, brawling, strife, dispute, and contention;
thus too one engages in dispute in the world by setting oneself above others.
Or else, one engages in quarreling, brawling, strife, dispute, and contention with another who sets themselves above others through their doctrine.
“You do not understand this Dhamma and Discipline... [etc.
...or unravel it if you are able.
In this way too, he brings about dispute in the world.
"Having abandoned all determinations":
"Determinations" refers to the sixty-two types of views.
Having abandoned, relinquished, renounced, forsaken, rejected, dispelled, brought to an end, and reduced to non-existence—all these determinations of views—[this is what is meant].
Having abandoned all disputes,
a person does not create strife in the world.
He does not engage in quarreling, he does not engage in brawling, he does not engage in contention, he does not engage in dispute, and he does not create strife.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Aggivessana, a bhikkhu whose mind is thus liberated does not agree with anyone, nor does he dispute with anyone; he employs the common parlance used in the world without clinging to it.
*Jantu* means a being, a person, a youth, a man, an individual, a soul, a creature, a living being, a human, a mortal, and a man.
"In the world"— in the world of the lower realms …pe… in the world of the sense bases—
a person does not create a rift while looking at the world.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Standing upon judgment and being himself negligent,
he brings about dispute in the world above;
having abandoned all forms of judgment,”
“A person does not create enmity in the world.
Thus ends the twelfth exposition, the *Cūḷabyūhasutta-niddesa*.
